Autoresearch

Turn Claude Code, OpenCode, OpenAI Codex, pi, or Muse into an improvement engine that doesn't stop.

It comes from Karpathy's autoresearch: constraint plus mechanical metric plus autonomous iteration equals compounding gains.

"Set the GOAL → The agent runs the LOOP → You wake up to results"

You don't need AGI. You need a goal, a metric, and a loop that never quits.

Claude Code, OpenCode, OpenAI Codex, pi, and Muse all get the core skill, the bundled runtime, installation, and verification surface. Hook guardrails ship for Claude Code (native hooks) and pi (extension events).

Fork-and-flush: metric loops climb off plateaus the way Cai et al. (arXiv:2610.07447) do. At 33% and 66% of the budget, or after 5 iterations with no keep, the loop forks fresh-context branches from the best commit so far, runs each briefly, and keeps the winner. Half the branches pick their own ideas (randomness). The other half each get a distinct experiment from a stateless Advisor that reads the results log (Zhang et al., arXiv:2610.07625). Guided: R sets the split. When the loop hits a plateau, the orchestrator answers with FORK before it gives up. See guide/autoresearch.md.

Bumblebee collects inventory from package, extension, and developer-tool metadata on macOS and Linux developer endpoints. It reads only.

It answers one narrow supply-chain question: when an advisory names a package, extension, or version, which developer machines show a match in their on-disk metadata right now?

SBOMs tell you what shipped. EDR tells you what ran or touched the network. Supply-chain response usually needs a third view: the messy local state sitting in lockfiles, package-manager metadata, extension manifests, and supported developer-tool configs.

Bumblebee turns that scattered state into structured NDJSON component records. Hand it an exposure catalog and it flags exact matches, so responders who already know what they're looking for can run read-only exposure checks.

Mean verifier reward: +21.12 pp

SkillsBench tests whether AI agents can use Skills to finish professional tasks across different domains. It asks a simple question: how much better does a model get at complex real-world work when you hand it specialized Skills?

We wanted to know how that holds up in production, where a lot of Skills sit installed at once. So we adapted SkillsBench into a large-scale multi-Skill setting. The original setup gave each task only the one Skill tied to it. Ours runs every task in a global environment holding all 195 specialized Skills, with everything else left alone. Now the agent has to find the right Skills on its own, pick them, and string them into a workflow that gets the job done.

We benchmarked vibeskills v4.1.0 on SkillsBench, using DeepSeekV4Flash-VE and OpenHands as the baseline evaluation setup. Against the baseline without vibeskills, vibeskills lifted the mean verifier reward by 21.12 percentage points, while cutting token consumption by 29.6% and tool calls by 33.1%.

It works in any Git repo with no setup.
